Outlawing Islam: An Essential Defense of Our Nation’s Social Fabric

Islam represents an existential threat to the social cohesion, legal foundations, and cultural continuity of our country. Multicultural policies that treated Islam as just another belief system have instead enabled demographic and institutional fragmentation that weakens the foundations of trust and cooperation any society requires.

Because the ideology is immutable, piecemeal accommodations have proven worse than useless. They signal weakness, encourage further demands, and allow the next generation to be raised under the same supremacist framework. Historical patterns of Islamic expansion—through conversion under pressure, demographic takeover, or outright conquest—repeat whenever demographic conditions allow. Surveys showing minority support for blasphemy laws, opposition to homosexuals in public life, and preference for religious law over national law confirm that the problem is structural rather than a matter of bad individuals who can simply be educated away. Existing citizens who identify as Muslim must be required to make a formal, public renunciation of the faith—through a legal process akin to other ideological disavowals required in times of national security crisis—pledging sole allegiance to the Constitution and secular law. Those who refuse face graduated criminal penalties: fines and mandatory civic education for initial violations, escalating to imprisonment for continued adherence, proselytizing, or leadership in Islamic organizations. Gentle tolerance has already produced visible erosion in countries with longer exposure; continuing the experiment guarantees deeper division and eventual conflict. Religious freedom is a noble principle, but it is not a suicide pact. It presumes reciprocal acceptance of pluralistic norms. When a system explicitly rejects reciprocity—commanding dominance over the unbeliever and death or social death for leaving the fold—it forfeits the protections it claims.

Our country must choose: maintain the fiction that all religions are interchangeable and watch the social contract dissolve under incompatible value systems, or act decisively to remove the incompatible one. Forcing renunciation or imposing penalties is not religious persecution in the classic sense; it is enforcement of the basic rule that no group may use the tolerance of the host society to subvert its foundational order.
